newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. Holocaust author admits faults to Germans.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Holocaust author admits faults to Germans.

text.p: An outspoken American Holocaust scholar who has upset and angered Germans by branding them as "Hitler's Willing Executioners" has conceded to his many critics that his controversial new book was flawed.

Harvard University sociologist Daniel Goldhagen, at his first public appearance in Germany since his book appeared, agreed his stark portrayal of ordinary Nazi-era Germans as zealots gripped by a drive to kill Jews was overdrawn.

His admission on Wednesday evening was a surprise twist in a heated transatlantic debate that Goldhagen, 37, has stirred up by claiming to have the real explanation for how a civilised nation like Germany could have killed six million Jews.

The debate about his best-selling book and the unusual public interest in his week-long book tour in Germany also showed how the Holocaust can still haunt this country half a century after it happened.

After listening to a panel of five German historians and journalists object to his blanket condemnation of their people, Goldhagen said: "I agree with the criticism. Of course not everything was exactly as I described in the basic model."

Several of the 400 Germans in the audience said they were disappointed that Goldhagen, who has vehemently defended his book and blasted his German critics in print, simply agreed with some key objections when discussing them in person.

"That bothered me," said Sy Esterer, a public relations executive. "I was astonished to see how he conceded so many points and then changed the subject," high school student Bele Freudenberg commented.

Goldhagen, the son of a Romanian Jew who survived the Holocaust, argued in "Hitler's Willing Executioners" that pre-1945 Germans were gripped by a unique "eliminationist anti-Semitism" and gladly took part in the "Final Solution."
Most who did not kill Jews themselves would have if given the chance, he argues in the hard-hitting book which appeared in German translation last month.

About his interpretation, which panelist Goetz Aly -- another Holocaust expert -- called "shaky," Goldhagen said: "I thought at the time it would be sufficient. I agree a more differentiated picture should ultimately be drawn."

While other Holocaust historians stress the virulence of anti-Semitism in pre-war Germany, they also look at Germany's defeat in the First World War and the turmoil of the 1920s as factors prompting Germans to seek a scapegoat.
"In retrospect, I should have written more about (that)," said Goldhagen when panelists pointed this out.

The panelists, who sat at black-draped tables in a stage setting as sombre as a wake, were so polite expressing their criticisms that the moderator had to urge them to speak out. Goldhagen spoke English while the others spoke in German.

Hannes Heer, a Hamburg historian who has documented the Wehrmacht's role in slaughtering Jews on the Eastern Front, even publicly apologised for a scathing review of Goldhagen's book he had published in a Berlin newspaper that morning. "I didn't mean to hurt his feelings," he explained.

Oskar Schapiro, a retired Jewish businessman who fled Germany in 1937 and fought in the British army against the Nazis, said he left the two-hour debate hardly more enlightened about the causes of the Holocaust than when he arrived for it.
"I missed a clear explanation of how German anti-Semitism was supposed to be unique," said Schapiro, 75. "Goldhagen overlooks many central issues in German history."
